title: Middle East flare-up to boost supply chain stress
gist: Oxford Economics expects a more drawn-out Middle East conflict after renewed US-Iran tensions effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz again, driving near-term supply-chain stress concentrated in Asia while sulphuric acid and refined oil product (diesel, jet fuel) prices rise, though US and German strategic reserves keep the helium market buffered.

themes.theme: Strait of Hormuz closure and conflict outlook

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects a more drawn-out Middle East conflict following the recent flare-up in US-Iran tensions, resulting in a long-term reduction in the level of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Investors should model a persistently elevated freight/insurance risk premium on Hormuz-transiting cargo rather than a quick resolution.
insights.quote: We expect a more drawn-out Middle East conflict, with a long-term reduction in the level of shipping through the Strait.

insights.claim: The recent flare-up in US-Iran tensions has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz again, marking a renewed disruption to this key shipping chokepoint.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A second effective closure signals the chokepoint risk is recurring, not one-off, raising the case for durable hedges on oil and shipping exposure.
insights.quote: The recent flare-up in US-Iran tensions has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz again
insights.locator: The recent flare-up in US-Iran tensions...

insights.claim: Supply-chain stress will increase in the near term and remain at a more elevated level than Oxford Economics had previously anticipated.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The forecast is a revision upward from a prior, less stressed baseline, implying investors should re-rate near-term supply-chain risk higher.
insights.quote: Supply-chain stress will increase in the near-term and remain at a more elevated level than previously anticipated.

insights.claim: Acute supply pressures from the conflict will remain more concentrated in Asia, while Europe and the US will see smaller, more price-driven impacts rather than physical shortages.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Asian manufacturers and importers face greater physical-disruption risk, while Western exposure is more of an inflation/cost pass-through story to watch via input prices.
insights.quote: Acute supply pressures will remain more concentrated in Asia, with smaller and more price-driven impacts in Europe and the US.

themes.theme: Commodity price pressures from the flare-up

insights.claim: Sulphuric acid prices have continued to increase, with especially sharp increases in Asia driven by heavy reliance on Middle Eastern exports compounded by China's export ban.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The combination of a Middle East supply disruption and China's export ban creates a specific, trackable squeeze in the sulphuric acid market that could pressure downstream industries (e.g., fertilizers, metals processing) reliant on Asian supply.
insights.quote: Sulphuric acid prices have continued to increase. A heavy reliance on Middle Eastern exports, compounded by China’s export ban, has driven especially sharp increases in Asia.
insights.locator: Sulphuric acid prices have continued to increase.

insights.claim: Refined oil product prices, particularly diesel and jet fuel, have crept up since the renewal of US-Iran tensions.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Rising diesel and jet fuel costs are an early, trackable inflation channel from the conflict, relevant to airline and freight cost forecasts.
insights.quote: Refined oil product prices have also crept up since the renewal in US-Iran tensions, particularly for diesel and jet fuel.
insights.locator: Refined oil product prices have also crept up...

insights.claim: Despite the broader disruption, significant strategic inventory held in the US and Germany means the global helium market still retains solid buffers.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Unlike sulphuric acid and refined oil products, helium is not an immediate near-term chokepoint risk, so investors should differentiate commodity exposure rather than assume uniform stress across the board.
insights.quote: Despite the disruption, there is still a significant degree of strategic inventory in the US and Germany, meaning the global helium market still retains solid buffers.
